record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: How can researchers characterize the real cross-client distribution shifts that appear in real-world federated datasets, and use that understanding to build controlled but realistic non-IID benchmarks that stress-test algorithms under the kinds of heterogeneity seen in deployment?

evidence.quote: Real-world federated learning datasets likely contain a mixture of these effects, and the characterization of cross-client differences in real-world partitioned datasets is an important open question. ... A better understanding of the nature of real-world non-IID datasets will allow for the construction of controlled but realistic non-IID datasets for testing algorithms and assessing their resilience to different degrees of client heterogeneity.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the federated learning setting in which a population of clients $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ each hold a local data distribution $P_i$ over an input-output space $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$, and the global learning task concerns the mixture $P = \sum_{i=1}^N w_i P_i$ for client weights $w_i \ge 0$ with $\sum_i w_i = 1$. Cross-client heterogeneity (non-IID-ness) can arise from several distinct mechanisms, including: (i) feature distribution skew, where the marginals $P_i(x)$ differ but $P_i(y \mid x)$ is shared; (ii) label distribution skew, where $P_i(y)$ differs but $P_i(x \mid y)$ is shared; (iii) concept drift, where $P_i(y \mid x)$ differs across clients while $P_i(x)$ is shared; (iv) concept shift, where $P_i(x \mid y)$ differs while $P_i(y)$ is shared; and (v) quantity skew, where the local sample sizes $n_i$ differ substantially.

Develop a quantitative framework that:

1. Defines measurable statistics $\{T_k(P_1, \dots, P_N)\}$ that decompose the heterogeneity present in a real-world federated dataset into contributions from the mechanisms (i)–(v) above (and possibly others, such as temporal drift within a client).

2. Estimates these statistics from samples and applies the framework to representative real-world partitioned datasets (e.g., user-keyed text, image, or sensor data) to characterize the actual mixture of effects observed in deployment.

3. Specifies a generative procedure $\mathcal{G}(\theta)$ — parameterized by a vector $\theta$ controlling the magnitudes of mechanisms (i)–(v) — that produces synthetic federated benchmarks whose statistics $\{T_k\}$ provably match (in expectation, up to a prescribed tolerance) those measured on real datasets, while also allowing controlled interpolation between IID and extreme heterogeneity regimes.

4. Demonstrates that the resulting controlled benchmarks are predictive: i.e., the relative performance of federated optimization algorithms on $\mathcal{G}(\theta_{\text{real}})$ correlates (in a precise, reported sense) with their performance on the corresponding real-world federated datasets, for a representative class of algorithms such as FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, and personalized variants.

The problem is to provide such a characterization and benchmark-construction methodology, together with the analyses establishing properties (1)–(4).
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of fully characterizing real-world cross-client distribution shifts and building controlled, realistic non-IID federated benchmarks remains an active and open research direction. Subsequent works (e.g., LEAF, FedScale, NIID-Bench, Flamby) have proposed partial taxonomies and benchmarks based on Dirichlet label-skew sampling or specific real datasets, but no widely accepted framework matches the empirical mixture of feature/label/concept shifts seen in deployment, and recent surveys continue to list realistic non-IID benchmarking as an unresolved challenge.

status_evidence.title: NIID-Bench: Federated Learning on Non-IID Data Silos
status_evidence.snippet: Introduces a benchmark with several synthetic non-IID partitioning strategies (label skew, feature skew, quantity skew) but acknowledges these are stylized rather than directly matched to real cross-client shifts.
status_evidence.claim: Partial progress: synthetic non-IID partitioning strategies have been proposed, but they are stylized rather than calibrated to real-world heterogeneity.

status_evidence.title: FedScale: Benchmarking Model and System Performance of Federated Learning at Scale
status_evidence.snippet: Provides realistic federated datasets at scale but does not provide a quantitative decomposition of heterogeneity mechanisms or a parameterized generator matched to them.
status_evidence.claim: Realistic federated datasets exist, but a controlled generator matched to measured real heterogeneity is not provided.

status_evidence.title: Flamby: Datasets and Benchmarks for Cross-Silo Federated Learning in Realistic Healthcare Settings
status_evidence.snippet: Provides real cross-silo healthcare datasets with natural heterogeneity, noting that quantitative characterization of the underlying distribution shifts is still lacking.
status_evidence.claim: Recent benchmarks emphasize that quantitative characterization of real cross-client shifts is still an open need.
